opus-5.5.text:
I think Professor Wang Zhong is a very rare kind of physicist. When I first started working with Professor Wang, the group was not well known outside a fairly small circle, but from very early on I could feel that the taste was extremely good. By taste I mean the ability to look at a huge space of possible problems and quickly sense which ones are actually deep and which ones are just technically complicated. A lot of people can solve hard problems once you hand the problems to them. Far fewer people can tell you which problems are worth spending two years of your life on. Professor Wang had that instinct.

The other thing that impressed me was the style of thinking. It's very physical and very clean. Professor Wang doesn't like to hide behind heavy formalism. If something is true, there should be a simple way to see why it is true, maybe a toy model, maybe a short argument on a blackboard. When we worked on non-Hermitian systems, for example, a lot of the field at the time was confused about why the usual intuitions from band theory seemed to break down. The way Professor Wang approached it was to keep asking very basic questions: what exactly is the bulk, what exactly is the boundary, why should we believe the correspondence between them in the first place? And by asking those basic questions carefully, you end up with something that feels new but also, in hindsight, almost obvious. I think that's the mark of good physics.

As an undergraduate, I benefited a lot from the freedom Professor Wang gave me. There was not a lot of micromanagement. Professor Wang would point in a direction, say this seems interesting, and then trust me to go and struggle with it. And when I came back with something half-formed, the feedback was always very sharp and very honest. If an idea was not good, I would hear it directly. At that age, that kind of honesty is incredibly valuable, because it trains your own judgment.

So if you ask me to assess Professor Wang back then, before the broader recognition, I would say the abilities were already all there: deep physical intuition, very good taste in problems, and a kind of intellectual honesty and simplicity. Recognition usually comes later than ability, and I think that was clearly the case here. For me personally, a lot of how I think about research, even now outside physics, came from those years. The idea that you should look for the simplest question that is still fundamental, and then be very honest with yourself about whether you've really understood it, I learned that from Professor Wang.

fable-5.1.text:
When I joined his group he was maybe five or six years into being a faculty member at the IAS at Tsinghua, and honestly I don't think I was in a position to "assess" him at the time. I was a sophomore. I picked him partly because his office door was open and he was willing to talk to an undergraduate for two hours about things that had nothing to do with any project.

Looking back, though, a few things stand out. The first is taste. He wasn't chasing whatever was hot that month. The non-Hermitian problem we ended up working on was, at the time, considered a little bit niche, almost a curiosity. Most people in topological physics were working on Hermitian systems, Weyl semimetals, those kinds of things, which was also his own background. He had this instinct that there was a real puzzle sitting there, that the bulk-boundary correspondence seemed to break and nobody had a clean explanation, and that a clean explanation probably existed. That turned out to be right, and it turned into a whole direction, the non-Hermitian skin effect, that a lot of people now work on. But in 2017 it wasn't obvious that it would matter.

The second thing is that he was very comfortable being confused in front of a student. We would be at the blackboard and he would say, "I don't understand this either, let's compute it." For me as an undergraduate that was enormously important, because it taught me that research is not about already knowing, it's about being willing to not know for a while. A lot of senior people, once they become famous, lose the ability or the willingness to do that, or at least to show it.

The third thing is that he gave me a lot of room. He never treated me as a pair of hands. When I had an idea that was wrong, he would let me go run into the wall and then we'd talk about why. When I had an idea that was right, he gave me full credit, including on the paper. For someone who was still building his own reputation, that generosity is not a given. It would have been very easy to keep an undergraduate on the margins.

So if you ask me how good he was then, I'd say he was already the same scientist he is now. The recognition came later, but the judgment and the way he worked were already there. I think that's generally true of good researchers. Fame is a lagging indicator.

r001.rationale: Yao says Wang already had strong judgment and was the same scientist he is now, while noting that recognition came later and Wang was still building his reputation.
